questions.ask: Did price just set a new session high or low, or stall near one?
questions.why: The one opening state with positive held-out skill on the lane's own grading; it folds the opening-range break in as a label clause because the break carries almost nothing once the fresh extreme is known.

questions.ask: How steeply are same-day puts priced over calls against recent sessions at this minute?
questions.why: Skew was not missing from history after all: the tape's quotes rebuild it. Raw skew is the clock (it decays from 0.15 to 0.03 through the day), so only the clock rank is asked; the far-put wing rides as a clause.

questions.ask: Did the rest of the index gap the same way as the heavyweight that moved it?
questions.why: When one stock is the index, SPX's gap is not the market's gap; on earnings reaction days the reporter's gap held and drifted instead of fading, which gap_origin used to mislabel as thin overnight drift.
questions.skipped: held from its other lane only until 11:32 ET

questions.ask: Where did the open land against yesterday's high and low?
questions.why: An open outside yesterday's whole range meets no overhead or underfoot trade from the day before; it is a stronger vote than the gap alone and sets up a bigger morning.
questions.skipped: held from its other lane only until 11:32 ET

questions.ask: Did VIX open higher, in line or lower than the overnight gap would leave it?
questions.why: Raw overnight VIX just repeats the gap (corr -0.79); what is new is hedging demand beyond the price move, and it leans contrarian.
questions.skipped: held from its other lane only until 11:32 ET

questions.ask: What does the morning news brief add to this morning's gap?
questions.why: The brief is the only news read the station makes, but it mostly repeats the futures; asking what it adds keeps it from double-counting the gap. Only leans_against can add anything.
questions.skipped: held from its other lane only until 11:32 ET

questions.ask: Over the last 30 minutes, how did price move?
questions.why: The single carrier of the move's sign for code to cross with other answers (so it serves direction); code also folds the options into |move| tiers for the size book, where the strong tier sharpens the flat call. It is also the reading canary: its answer key is the label's own band.

questions.ask: Did the latest leg run with or against the day's side of yesterday's close?
questions.why: The 30-minute move alone predicts almost nothing; split by the day's side measured from yesterday's close, legs with the day tend to continue and legs against it tend to fade.

questions.ask: How was the last half hour's move made?
questions.why: Burst and choppy moves both leave price unsettled and bigger moves follow; clean moves continued before mid-afternoon and faded after, a clock interaction code weights by phase. The engine already computes path efficiency; no round-1 question read it.

questions.ask: Was the last 60 minutes one-way or two-way?
questions.why: An hour that moved one way without trading back through its own average has used up its one-sided flow and tends to give some back; the only chop measure that carried direction.

questions.ask: Did the last half hour move, and was its range narrow or wide?
questions.why: A flat net move hides a wide two-way hour; that state is flat far less often and carries more than double the both-ways whipsaw risk, so it pushes P(flat) down and tells code to trust direction less.

questions.ask: So far today, are the moves building or cancelling out?
questions.why: A description of the day so far, not a forecast: the old 'trending / mean_reverting' names invited a continuation call the data contradicts, so the options now describe the past and code learns the sign.

questions.ask: Is this morning's gap intact or being lost?
questions.why: Replaces gap_fill_state's unsigned options: 'holding' mixed gap-up and gap-down days, so the loop learned the summer's gap mix instead of the rule. Signed options each hold 15-35% of days, and the location-first wording follows the SNDK back-inside fix.

questions.ask: Will price trade back to yesterday's close within the next 60 minutes?
questions.why: A directly gradable forecast that feeds P(flat); asked only where it is uncertain.
questions.skipped: asleep: the gap down is still open, not losing ground

questions.ask: From the settled open to late morning, did price go with the gap or fill it?
questions.why: Overnight gaps get pulled back early, then the direction the overnight market voted for often comes back after noon; the side lives in the label and code applies it.

questions.ask: Is SPX's move from yesterday's close from the gap or built today?
questions.why: Round 1 measured the day only from the settled open, which carries no momentum on SPX; the move from yesterday's close does carry forward through midday, and the gap is the part that carries it.

questions.ask: What has price done with the first hour's range since?
questions.why: Ten options folded to five: each mirrored pair shared one effect across two thin cells, and the loop learns direction relative to the broken edge's side (still_forming is replaced by sleeping before the first hour ends).

questions.ask: Where is price against the usual move-from-the-open band for this minute?
questions.why: A trend-versus-noise read anchored at the higher and lower of the open and yesterday's close, averaged over the prior 14 sessions; kept as a regime read, not as the source strategy's Sharpe.

questions.ask: Where does the late push stand against yesterday's close?
questions.why: Yesterday's close is the level every desk marks into the close; a late push that stalls short of it or crosses and fails is a fade setup, and one that holds through it is a flip of the day's sign.
questions.skipped: not on its schedule at the 15:32 ET read

questions.ask: How busy was the last half hour against the same half hour on recent sessions?
questions.why: Recent realized movement is the best single forecaster of the next half hour's size; ranking it at the same clock removes the U-shape. Dividing by the straddle (round 1) cancelled most of that information, and coil_state's fixed cuts were the clock (coiled 0% at 10:00, 37% at 14:00).

questions.ask: Is the rest of today priced cheaper or richer than usual for this time of day?
questions.why: The one home for the live straddle and the 0DTE vol pop (sigma_live over anchor correlates 0.87 with this ratio); it absorbs today_vs_month's proxy form, and a one-day VIX clause joins once that series has a same-clock baseline.

questions.ask: How much has VIX moved as a share of its level?
questions.why: A VIX move adds to next-move size beyond the SPX move; fixed points break as VIX rises, so the move is a share of the level, and a share's size swings with the clock, so it is ranked against the same window at the same minute on the recent sessions (the owner's rule). vix_open_path folds in: its four-way split added nothing at 10 minutes.

questions.ask: How wide is the flat band against SPX's typical move over the horizon?
questions.why: The flat leg is most of the up/flat/down score; the clock knows the hour but not whether today is quiet. One number tells JEV how hard 'flat' is to hit.

questions.ask: How does today's range so far compare with a normal day's pace?
questions.why: Day energy. The figure is today's range over a one-sigma move from the morning ruler for the time elapsed, not 'the range the options market priced' (the ruler overstates realized about 2.5x), so the label says what it measures; its rank against the same minute on the recent sessions, not a fixed line, says whether today runs fast or slow for the hour.

questions.ask: Is SPY's quote wider or thinner than usual for this time of day?
questions.why: The only equity liquidity read: a wide quote on the most liquid ETF means market makers are pulling back, which comes before bigger swings, clearest in the afternoon. It says nothing about direction.

questions.ask: Did the last 30 minutes reprice the rest of today richer or cheaper than the clock?
questions.why: The straddle's level is straddle_vs_clock; its change against pure time decay is the market repricing the afternoon, a size read the level hides.

questions.ask: Will price trade at the day's volume-weighted average within the next 30 minutes?
questions.why: A directly gradable reach forecast for the flat bucket: the day's average is the level most intraday flow trades back to.

questions.ask: Did VIX move more or less fearfully than the SPX move explains?
questions.why: Fear showing up in VIX before price is how an unscheduled headline often appears first. Size is the stable part; the direction lean is unstable, so the why no longer calls it the best direction candidate and code learns any sign.

questions.ask: Did VVIX stir beyond what the VIX and SPX moves explain?
questions.why: Raw VVIX mostly repeats VIX (corr 0.74-0.76); the leftover flags hedging in the VIX options market that neither price nor VIX shows yet, often the first sign a pinned afternoon is about to break.

questions.ask: Did SPX move, and did VVIX rise or fall with it?
questions.why: VIX nearly always rises on a drop, but VVIX rising or falling separates a panicked selloff (bounces) from an orderly one (continues), and flags unstable rallies. Replaces the deferred spot_vix_pairing.

questions.ask: Did nine-day fear rise or fall against the VIX?
questions.why: VIX9D's own change repeats VIX (corr 0.93) and the level gap is constant within the day; the shift in the gap is the only new intraday piece.

questions.ask: Did downside protection get dearer or cheaper than the SPX move explains?
questions.why: Traders read 'puts getting bid' as a warning; only the part price does not explain is new. It is independent of the VIX residual (corr -0.007) and leans the other way, so the two must never be blended into one 'fear' sentence.

questions.ask: Did same-day at-the-money vol move more or less than the price move explains?
questions.why: The 0DTE version of vix_vs_price at the hour horizon showed a clean size effect in the opposite direction: an IV bid beyond price came before calmer trading.
questions.skipped: missing vol.atm_iv_residual

questions.ask: Where does this moment sit against today's scheduled events?
questions.why: Code needs the phase. released_before_open could never fire (the calendar left out pre-open releases); the calendar now carries pre-open, 10:00 and Fed-speaker tiers, and the Fed-speaker window is the one scheduled slice of the dark news gap.
questions.skipped: asleep: every scheduled event today came out more than 120 minutes ago

questions.ask: Where does today sit in the cycle of major scheduled releases?
questions.why: Eve afternoons trade at about a quarter of normal size and post-release sessions were among the narrowest on file; the clock and sigma cannot see tomorrow's calendar. The post_release_calm forecast folds in here.

questions.ask: Is today's priced move swollen or compressed, and is an event behind it?
questions.why: On event days every sigma and straddle label under-reads moves before the release and over-reads after; before the release the tape is not swollen, the ruler is. Code can use the answer to trust or rescale the size answers.

questions.ask: How is the VIX curve shaped against its usual?
questions.why: A day-level regime read: the inversions are definitions and come first; below them the curve is judged only by its rank against the same minute on the recent sessions (the owner's rule), so the fixed near-flat line and its 'flat' option are gone; the nine-day inversion is the one inversion that actually happened.
questions.skipped: a day constant: asked at 10:02 ET and held

questions.ask: What kind of selloff is this stress day?
questions.why: Selloff days are where intraday momentum is strongest and where a VIX retreat off the high is the classic turn; none of the 59 calm sessions reaches this state for long, so the question sleeps until it matters.
questions.skipped: missing vol.stress_path

questions.ask: Which way do today's same-day options books lean at the current price?
questions.why: Replaces gamma_sign_trust with words that describe what code computed (the call-vs-put gamma balance at price), so JEV's 'long gamma pins' prior never fires; split books are where reversion to VWAP and of the 30-minute move is measurable, and the two split directions are not symmetric.

questions.ask: How far is price from the gamma flip?
questions.why: In this data the sign is price's side of the flip, and the distance carries the direction lean the plain long/short word flattens; asking the distance removes the textbook damping prior. The deferred flip_position_cross becomes an option (crosses are rare because the flip travels with price).

questions.ask: Did price move, and which way do the options books lean?
questions.why: The single cross of the move with the book. It repeats much of the move (NMI 0.865), but the one cell that separates is measurable, and the split cells now carry a side because under split books the move reverses.

questions.ask: How does the options book's balance pair with the pace?
questions.why: The book's calming effect exists only after the opening hours; asking it all day blurred it into nothing, which made the sign look inverted. The pace input is now the last half hour, not the whole day's pace.

questions.ask: Where does the gamma sit in today's book and the week's?
questions.why: Before noon today's same-day book holds about a third of the gamma dealers hedge; the week's book fires on more days and disagrees with today's on a third of reads. No 'lid or floor' wording: the two old texts contradicted each other. Each book is now judged by its third against the same book at this minute on recent sessions (owner rule 2026-09-27), not the 40%-60% even band the evidence was measured on: more above or below price than usual, never which side holds most.

questions.ask: Is price seated on today's heaviest strike, near it, or away?
questions.why: The one tradeability signal that beats the clock on SPX: a seated, gripping pin means a flatter next half hour. It is a speed limit, not a magnet, until the last half hour (see settle_pull_side). Grip is ranked at the same clock because it climbs all day.

questions.ask: How tight is the box between the heaviest call-side and put-side strikes?
questions.why: A tight standing box is a quiet read; the morning/later split re-asked the clock that code already blends, so it is gone.

questions.ask: How did the heaviest strikes move over the last 30 minutes?
questions.why: Keeps the one part of walls_vs_move that changes within the day and drops the repeat of the move (77% of its answers were no_move); code crosses it with the move.

questions.ask: What happened at the heavy strike price touched?
questions.why: Signed options so the loop learns direction; no_touch (78% of reads) is removed by gating, so the default answer never enters the weights.
questions.skipped: missing levels.wall_touch_effort

questions.ask: Are market makers defending the nearest heavily hit strike or leaving it?
questions.why: The only order-book read with any support here; it reads the options book's refill, not SPY's top of book.

questions.ask: Which side of the day's average price is SPX, and do the books agree?
questions.why: Every option carries a side. Whether a departure from the average comes back depends on the books agreeing, not on the long/short word, which just repeats which side of the flip price is on. The stretch size and minutes since the last touch ride in the label.

questions.ask: Where is price against yesterday's value area, and which way is today going?
questions.why: Traders judge acceptance against yesterday's fair value. Today's move alone predicts nothing here, but a rally that stays below yesterday's value tends to fail and strength above value tends to keep going. Round 1 used only yesterday's high and low.

questions.ask: What is price doing at yesterday's high or low?
questions.why: Folded: the high and low mirrors share one table with direction learned relative to the edge's side (named in the label), and the location-first wording avoids the SNDK back-inside misread.

questions.ask: Has price just crossed a round level, or is it pressing one?
questions.why: Almost every SPX trader marks the big round numbers; order data shows stops cluster just past them and speed the move once crossed. The levels are also the big SPXW strikes, so it goes on the overlap list with the wall questions.

questions.ask: Is a level-break setup armed, and which way?
questions.why: The station arms this setup only when the book leans to puts and price was just turned back at a named level; its direction comes from the level, not the last move, and it survives a momentum control. It is the usable part of level_reclaim, which never fired.
questions.skipped: asleep: no break armed, and none expired or was called off in the last 30 minutes

questions.ask: Did option or SPY activity come with a price move?
questions.why: Heavy trading that is not moving price is absorption; unproven, so it stays live and goes on the overlap list with realized_vs_clock.

questions.ask: Does breadth side with the last half hour's move?
questions.why: Template for every 'X vs the move' cross: sign-free options leave direction to price_move_5way alone, so the combiner does not count the move again inside each cross (SNDK closes_agree was retired for exactly this). Code multiplies agree/against by the move's sign.
questions.skipped: missing breadth.upvol_share_30m

questions.ask: Since the open, has volume been lopsided, rotating or leaning?
questions.why: A rotating-day read for the flat bucket; unproven, so live.
questions.skipped: missing breadth.day_upvol_share

questions.ask: Did the NYSE tick lean to buying or selling more than usual for this half hour?
questions.why: Two questions counted the same TICK side, and raw TICK sits below zero most of the time (median share above zero 0.33), so both answered 'selling' in a rising market. One question, measured against the usual for the clock.

questions.ask: Did breadth confirm SPX's new session extreme?
questions.why: The classic narrow-push tell. The megacap basket almost never splits (QQQ confirmed 97 of 101 SPX highs), while small caps split about in half, so IWM replaces it; no_new_extreme is removed by gating.
questions.skipped: missing price.session_extreme_recent, breadth.at_extremes

questions.ask: Is SPX's move since the open backed by net buying in its own stocks?
questions.why: A day move made on the members' own net selling is carried by a few heavy names or futures, and it stalled or turned more often. $VOLSPD is S&P 500 up-minus-down volume, not Nasdaq breadth as round 1 and the feed probe said.
questions.skipped: missing breadth.members_net_day

questions.ask: Has net volume in S&P 500 stocks been stronger or weaker than across the NYSE?
questions.why: The two tallies usually agree (0.91); when the index's own members lag the whole exchange, big-cap selling is hidden by ADRs, funds and smaller listings.
questions.skipped: missing breadth.members_net_day

questions.ask: Since the release, has NYSE volume switched sides?
questions.why: A release that flips which stocks carry the volume has changed the day's story; one that leaves the breadth side alone was noise.
questions.skipped: asleep: no in-session release in the last 120 minutes

questions.ask: Did volume run heavier in rising or falling stocks than their count suggests?
questions.why: TRIN's information that up-volume share and the advance count each miss: whether the money is concentrated on one side.

questions.ask: Did the typical stock move with the index, or did the biggest stocks carry it?
questions.why: Beta-adjusted: raw RSP moves only 0.66x SPY, so the raw gap made every big move look narrow. Sign-free so the move is not counted twice.

questions.ask: Did semiconductors run ahead of the index, and which way?
questions.why: Chips lead the AI-weighted index; the side is in the option, not a product with the move.

questions.ask: Did the sector funds move together with the index?
questions.why: Index variance is component variance times correlation; rotation under a flat index is the best-grounded chop idea outside price.

questions.ask: How did the largest index stocks move together over the last 30 minutes?
questions.why: Concentration flag. one_name almost never fired at the old rule (1.5% of windows); the basket now comes from weights, with TSLA in and Alphabet's two share classes combined.
questions.skipped: missing leaders.megacap_cohesion_30m

questions.ask: Which part of the index did the moving over the last 30 minutes?
questions.why: Cap-weighted split: is one group the index today. A tug of war under a pinned index is megacap_pull_at_pin's case, now crossed by code with magnet_seat instead of a pin-gated question that was not_pinned on over 95% of reads.
questions.skipped: missing leaders.pull_vs_rest_30m

questions.ask: Since the open, have tech or small caps led the index?
questions.why: Leadership only shows over hours; the 30-minute version carries nothing and repeats move_breadth, so this is deliberately day-long. The label says who led and code learns the sign (textbook reads small-cap leadership as risk-on; this tape did the opposite).

questions.ask: Are Treasuries ahead of the index, and which way?
questions.why: When Treasury prices run ahead of what the index's move would match and the two have been trading together, the index tends to follow; the label states today's link sign, so it works in either stock-bond regime. $TNX bars stop at 15:00, so TLT or /ZN is the source.

questions.ask: Did oil move further than its usual link to the index explains?
questions.why: Oil has moved against stocks in this tape; an oil jump the index has not absorbed has come before weakness. Code learns the sign; the label never says bullish or bearish.

questions.ask: Are bonds, credit, oil, gold and the euro ahead of the index, and which way?
questions.why: One pooled read catches macro repricing the index has not joined yet, without near-duplicate single-asset questions. It replaces cross_asset_confirm, whose UUP feed is broken and whose risk-off signs are wrong in this tape, and absorbs gold.
questions.skipped: missing xasset.macro_gap_30min

questions.ask: Did risk-on sectors beat or trail the defensive ones?
questions.why: Sector risk appetite beneath the index; unproven, live.

questions.ask: Which part of the expiry cycle is today?
questions.why: SPX lists an expiry every day, but the monthly is morning-settled (its gamma is gone after Friday's open) while the quarter-end book is close-settled. Split out of calendar_flow_day so the one-window rule no longer hides 09-30.
questions.skipped: not on its schedule at the 15:32 ET read

questions.ask: Which month-turn flow is in play for the rest of today?
questions.why: Turn of the month is the one calendar window with a local direction tilt; the rebalance side is worded as a close-and-next-day flow, which matches the published mechanism. It replaces calendar_flow_day's regime role and the sign lives in the options.
questions.skipped: missing flows.rebalance_side

questions.ask: What has price done since the last hour's shock?
questions.why: News with no feed shows up as a burst far bigger than the tape usually moves at that time of day; volatility clusters, so a fresh or round-tripped shock means a busier next half hour, even when the net move looks small. Every window is ranked against the biggest five-minute move of the same hour on recent sessions, so an hour of windows does not throw up a shock by chance.
questions.skipped: asleep: no five-minute move in the last 60 minutes passed the shock rule (larger than the biggest five-minute move of the hour to that minute, or from the settled open when that is shorter, on every one of up to the last 20 sessions); the largest was 0.09 sigma, larger than the biggest five-minute move of the hour to that minute on 11 of the last 19 sessions

questions.ask: Where did the shock take price against today's range?
questions.why: A burst that runs stops through the day's extreme with nothing behind it tends to snap back; a burst inside the range is more often real repricing. The side lives in the label.
questions.skipped: missing shock.burst, shock.vs_day_range

questions.ask: What has price done since the first reaction to the latest release or burst?
questions.why: Unscheduled headlines are SPX's largest move source and there is no feed, but the burst they leave is visible. Widening the trigger from the calendar to any burst lets the question fire about once a day and be graded; on Fed days the reaction starts at the press conference, where the real move came.

questions.ask: Did VIX overreact or shrug at the shock?

questions.ask: Which way has price run since the early afternoon?
questions.why: In the last half hour the closing auction undoes the afternoon's run; the 90-minute leg is the signal, not round 1's 30-minute leg or the day move. Earlier in the afternoon the same leg continues, so code learns a per-slot mapping. The day move from yesterday's close and the range position ride in the label (close_stretch merged: they add nothing once the leg is known).

questions.ask: Where does today's heaviest strike sit against price before the settle?
questions.why: SPXW settles on the 16:00 print and dealer rehedging into settlement pulls the close toward the heavy strike, but locally only after 15:30 and through the 15:50 auction; the ruler for 'how far' shrinks all afternoon because today's options die at the close, so distance is counted in remaining straddles.

questions.ask: Where does the charm wall sit against price?
questions.why: Unproven, not disproven, so live on a 30-minute horizon (what the evidence measured); the charm sign never varies (negative on 50/50 days), so only the location is asked, with remaining straddles in the label.

questions.ask: How heavy was trading in the last 30 minutes for this time of day?
questions.why: The closing auction is the day's biggest volume event; a heavy last half hour means programs are already working and the close moves further. It feeds P(flat) at the read where the clock baseline is weakest.

questions.ask: Since the Fed press conference began, has price extended or reversed the statement's move?
questions.why: On both FOMC days on disk the real move came during the press conference and lasted to the close; the statement's 15 minutes said little.

questions.ask: Has VIX drifted up, held or drifted down since the early afternoon?

questions.ask: Across the lane's last reads, is the day's move from the open still making new ground, stalled, or unwinding?
questions.why: A move that keeps making new ground read after read differs from one whose high came two reads ago; no single-window question says which read the extreme came at.

questions.ask: Across the lane's last reads, has breadth built behind the day's move, faded under it, or tracked it?
questions.why: breadth_day_regime judges one moment; a divergence is a sequence: price keeps going while the volume behind it slips read after read.

questions.ask: Did bitcoin run ahead of the index over the last half hour, and which way?
questions.why: The usual idea is that bitcoin is a fast risk gauge the index follows. Measured here, it runs the other way. When bitcoin has run ahead of the index in the last half hour, the index's next half hour leans slightly the opposite way. At the minute level the index leads bitcoin, not the reverse. The label reports the move and the link and does not say 'bitcoin leads', so the learning loop learns the sign.

questions.ask: Has bitcoin run ahead of the index the same way for three half-hours in a row?
questions.why: One half-hour of bitcoin drift can be noise. Three in a row in the same direction is a steadier sign that risk appetite outside stocks is moving differently from the index. The measured effect is small and, like btc_gap_30m, runs against bitcoin's direction.
questions.skipped: asleep: the last three half hours point different ways

questions.ask: Are bitcoin and the index trading together today more tightly than usual, or less?
questions.why: Bitcoin's tie to stocks comes and goes. Since 2020 the 60-session correlation of daily moves has run from -0.09 to 0.72. This year the 20-session figure fell from about 0.7 in March and April to 0.26 in August. A tight day says one risk mood is driving both markets. A loose day says bitcoin is on its own news, and its moves say little about stocks. This question tells the loop which days to trust the other bitcoin reads on.

questions.ask: Over the last week, has bitcoin been lagging the index or running ahead of it?
questions.why: The 'canary' idea is that bitcoin weakening while stocks hold up warns of a stock drop. The data does not support it. From 2020 to 2026, weeks when bitcoin lagged were followed by slightly better index days, not worse. The pattern was not stable in 2025-26. It is in the set because it is the most common bitcoin-for-stocks claim, and the loop should learn its sign rather than JEV assuming it.

questions.ask: How large was this morning's gap from yesterday's close?
questions.why: Gap size sets how busy the first half hour is; it says nothing about the next 10 minutes' direction, so it serves size only and is asked once instead of twelve identical times.

questions.ask: Which side of the settled open does the opening favour now?
questions.why: Replaces opening_drive's seven options with five signed ones: stalling and failed flipped sign between windows on 10-24 reads, and tested_then_reversed fired on 2 of 59 days.

questions.ask: Did price just set a new session high or low, or stall near one?
questions.why: The one opening state with positive held-out skill on the lane's own grading; it folds the opening-range break in as a label clause because the break carries almost nothing once the fresh extreme is known.

questions.ask: How contested has the settled open been so far?
questions.why: Repeated fights over the settled open mean two-way flow is active: the next 10 minutes run larger, even after a quiet 5 minutes, which moves weight out of the five-way flat bucket. Crossings pile up with the minutes since the open, so the count is judged against the same minute on the recent sessions, not a fixed count. Asked from 09:45, when ten minutes of path exist (open.chop and the tape unit go live then): at 09:40 five bars give 0 to 2 crossings and 2 already ranks top third. Crossings are small whole numbers and a tie is not beaten, so the thirds come out uneven (about 42/25/32% bottom/middle/top over 09:40-10:30 on 39 replayed days).

questions.ask: How busy is the opening for this time of day?
questions.why: The median of three 5-minute ranges is the lane's own outcome unit and forecasts the next 10 minutes better than the last 5 minutes, which also carries the stale 09:30 catch-up.

questions.ask: How choppy or one-way has the open been since the settled open?
questions.why: Owner decision #10 (2026-09-27): whether the open has been chopping around the settled open or travelling one way is a regime read the five-way call lacks; open_contested counts the fights over one level, this measures the whole path. Path efficiency falls with the minutes since the open, so it is judged against the same minute on the recent sessions, not a fixed line.

questions.ask: Since the open, has net volume leaned to buying or selling against a usual morning?
questions.why: The only opening input in review whose interval clears zero and holds after removing the price move; it is the 10-minute breadth read round 1 asked for, with the advance-decline thrust folded in. Each total is ranked against the same minute on recent sessions (owner rule 2026-09-27), no longer sized in usual swings against a fixed line.

questions.ask: Since the open, how one-sided has market-wide buying and selling been?
questions.why: Traders read opening TICK clusters as trend-day tells; the fixed plus-or-minus-1000 line may never fire on SPX (probe closes -829..+944), so the burst band is a same-minute percentile of bar highs and lows.

questions.ask: Which way did the large same-day option trades of the last 10 minutes lean?

questions.ask: How steeply are same-day puts priced over calls against recent sessions at this minute?

questions.ask: Did semiconductors or financials break away from the index in the last 10 minutes?
questions.why: Chips lead the AI-weighted index at the open; splitting the semis option by side lets the loop learn direction without the side hiding in the label.

questions.why: Overnight bonds reprice on news before cash stocks open; a gap that bonds did not match tends to trade back toward the bonds' side in the first hour. The sign and size of the link come from the last nights, never assumed. Bitcoin is its own question (btc_overnight_vs_futures).

questions.ask: Did bitcoin move further overnight than S&P futures did, and which way?
questions.why: Bitcoin trades through the night and reacts to the same risk news as stocks. If it has moved further than futures, the thought is that stocks have not caught up yet. The data says futures already have: bitcoin's overnight move sits inside the gap (rank correlation +0.63 with the SPX open gap) and adds nothing after 09:30. It is here so the learning loop can confirm that, and because the owner asked for bitcoin in the pre-open read.

questions.ask: After a big bitcoin weekend, did bitcoin keep going, hold, or turn back once S&P futures reopened?
questions.why: Bitcoin is the one big market that trades all weekend, so it shows first how risk appetite moved while stocks were shut. A peer-reviewed study (Mourey, Shahrour, Soiman, Finance Research Letters 2025) finds that weak crypto weekends predict weaker Mondays for stocks and strong ones do not, an effect that grew after the May 2022 LUNA collapse. That study measures Friday close to Monday close, and at 09:28 the futures gap already contains most of it. This question asks the part the gap does not show: whether bitcoin's weekend verdict is being confirmed or taken back since futures reopened.
